opener.heading: Week 8: Art Masters Studio 🎨
about: Azlyn starts Friday with three pots of paint and no green in the house. She mixes six colors before ten, names them herself, and her names run through the rest of the week. Saturday she tears and cuts a garden out of the junk mail. Sunday everyone in the house sits for a portrait and then gets built again in salt dough. Monday goes under the dining table, where she papers a cave and paints it with mud and cocoa. Tuesday is yarn, weaving and dyed pasta. Wednesday she takes the texture off half the street with a crayon, posts four of the results to four people and watches at least one door open.

Thursday gathers all of it. She hangs the week on a wall at her own eye level, writes the labels, cuts the tickets, and Joseph comes home at five having seen none of it. No holiday lands in these seven days, so the shape comes from the making and from what each day hands to the next one. February does the rest. The street is gray enough that a red door counts as a find, green is coming back into the flower beds while she is out looking for it, and the ground is soft enough to dig a color out of on Monday.
azlyn: Color mixing, done with her own hands. Three pots go on the table and six colors come off it, each one stirred and named by her.
Scissors. Thumb up through the top hole, two fingers below, and enough paper to waste while her wrist works the rest out.
Sorting by one rule. Red through the red slot, yellow through the yellow, and a reasoned argument for the awkward ones.
Threading and weaving. Over, under, over on a card loom, then pasta onto string, both hands meeting in front of her.
Drawing what she can see. A face counted out loud in the mirror first, then portraits of everyone in the house, including one who would not hold still.
you: Posting things through slots is a real developmental stage
Love is a word she's still working out the size of
"A long time ago" is as much history as she can hold
Threading is fine motor work that pays off at six
Children need to see the effect of their kindness
Anticipating someone else's future feeling is a big cognitive leap

opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 8 months this week. He crawls or shuffles after her, bangs two things together to hear what they do, and has arrived at stranger wariness, so he checks a new room from your shoulder before he takes it on.

days.title: Three Paints, Six Colors
days.prepTonight: Put the red, yellow and blue paint on the table with a white plate, an egg carton and Joseph's old shirt, and hide every other color you own.

opening.title: Only Three Paints
opening.need: red, yellow and blue paint · 1 white plate · 2 brushes · thick paper.
steps: Put out the three pots and nothing else. Let her paint whatever she wants with what is there.
She will ask for green. Tell her there is no green in the house and stay with that, however the next two minutes go.
Ask which two she thinks would get closest. Put a blob of each on the white plate, side by side, and leave them unstirred. Tell her you will finish it at 9:15.

main.title: Making Green
materials: Washable poster paint in red, yellow and blue
1 white plate or a white tile as the mixing palette
1 egg carton or ice cube tray for holding the new colors
2 brushes, one thin one wide
1 jam jar of water
Thick paper, 8–10 sheets
Paper towels
1 teaspoon
An old shirt of Joseph's as an apron
steps: Shirt on, water filled, paper towels within reach. The white plate is the only surface that matters, because color lies to you on brown card.
Start with her guess from this morning. Two teaspoons of yellow on the plate, then blue a quarter-spoon at a time, stirred in with the thin brush until she calls it green.
Scrape it into a cup of the egg carton. She owns green now.
Do red and yellow next, then red and blue. Each new color gets its own cup and its own stir.
Let her name every one out loud. Take mud, sunset and dark over anything off a paint chart, and use her names all day.
Hand her the paper and all six colors and leave her to paint.
main.tip: Add the dark color into the light one a spoonful at a time. Yellow tipped into blue gives you a jar of blue and a bad mood. Blue tipped into yellow gives you every green there is.

outside.title: The Gray Street Color Hunt
paras: February has bled the color out of the street, so go and hunt for what is left. A red front door, a green trash can, moss on a north-facing wall, somebody's crocuses up early in a front yard, the yellow line on the road. Count them out loud as she finds them. Ask which of the six she made this morning comes closest to each.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and bangs two things together to hear what they do. Give him a clean egg carton and a wooden spoon on the floor at the far end of the room while the wet paint stays up on the table. On the walk, wear him facing out. Stranger wariness has arrived this month, so keep him on you rather than in the stroller if anyone stops to talk.

second.title: Where the Colors Run
second.intro: Water carries paint further than a brush does. Wet the paper first and the colors travel on their own.
materials: Thick paper, 6 sheets
The mixed colors from this morning, thinned with water
1 wide soft brush
1 clean sponge for wetting the paper
1 baking tray or the draining board to work in
Paper towels
1 jam jar of water
steps: Set the tray on the table and lay one sheet inside it. Everything from here runs off the edges.
Thin the morning's colors with water until they drip off the brush in a stream instead of a blob.
Wet the whole sheet with the sponge until it shines, then mop the standing water off with paper towels.
Show her one drop. Loaded brush held above the paper, one touch, and the color opens out across the wet like ink.
Now a second color beside the first, close enough that the two edges meet. Green arrives where blue meets yellow.
Do a dry sheet for comparison. Same paint, hard edges, no travel. Let her say which she prefers.
Leave them flat where they are. Wet paper tears the moment you lift it, so nothing moves until dinner.
second.tip: She will keep going until every sheet is brown, because brown is where these end. Take the brush after five or six drops and call it finished.

alternatives: Three jars of water, food coloring and one pipette.
Sweet wrappers and cellophane held over each other at the window.
Ice cubes of colored water melting on a white plate.
outAgain: Playgroup, and take one of the morning's mixed-color paintings to give away
The park, for a run before the light goes
A friend's kitchen, if anyone will have two children and a bag of paint
The garden center, for the seed packet pictures and the warm greenhouse
Round the block with the stroller and no destination

aroundWorld.title: Mexico and the Alebrijes 🐉
paras: In Oaxaca and Mexico City, carvers make alebrijes: animals with the head of one creature, the wings of another and the tail of a third, painted in colors that fight each other on purpose. Pedro Linares dreamed them while he was ill in the 1930s and carved what he had seen. Whole families carve and paint them together now, and no two come out the same.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Mexican conchas are sweet buns with a colored sugar shell scored into a pattern on top. Buy a couple, or ice a plain bun and let Azlyn scratch a pattern in with a fork before it sets.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Alebrijes are carved from copal wood, which is soft enough to cut while the branch is still green.

days.krestonPM: At 8 months he settles into a room once he has checked it from your lap, so keep him facing you for the first ten minutes at playgroup. Stranger wariness at this age means he has worked out who his people are.

insight.headline: Discovery beats demonstration.
paras: You could have told her at 8:05 that blue and yellow make green. She would have believed you and lost it by Thursday. She stirred it herself, so what she holds is a rule she can run again on the next two colors. Researchers comparing direct instruction with guided discovery find the taught version wins on speed and the discovered version wins on transfer, which means the child uses it somewhere new. Your work was the setup. Three colors and no green in the house is a question she cannot walk away from, and the answer costs her a teaspoon and two minutes of stirring.

days.safety: Wet paint pots at floor level with an 8-month-old who crawls and mouths everything. Washable non-toxic paint only, lids back on between colors, and empty the paint water down the sink the moment she finishes. Never leave a full jar within his reach.

days.title: The Paper Garden
days.prepTonight: Put the week's junk mail, catalogs and magazines in a pile on the table with the glue stick, and find a shoebox with a lid for this afternoon.

opening.title: Tearing Up the Catalogue
opening.need: the pile of junk mail · 1 large sheet or a flattened box · masking tape.
steps: The junk mail you piled on the table last night is the morning's supply. Tip it onto the floor, sit down in the pile with her and pull pages out. Hands only, no scissors yet.
Ask her to find you green pages, then red ones, then yellow. Tear those into one heap per color.
Tape the big sheet flat to the table so it stops sliding about. It sits there in front of her until 9:15.

main.title: The Cut-Out Garden
materials: Junk mail, catalogs and magazines
Colored paper if you have it
1 pair of child-safe scissors
1 pair of adult scissors (adult only, kept high)
Glue stick, or flour-and-water paste in a saucer
1 large sheet: the back of wrapping paper or a flattened box
1 permanent marker
steps: Show her the hold once. Thumb up through the top hole, two fingers below, paper gripped in the other hand. Then stop talking about it.
No pencil lines and nothing to follow. She cuts into the colored heaps and finds out what comes off.
Name each piece as it lands. A long thin one is a leaf, a round one is a flower head, a raggedy one is a bush. Her names win.
Once she has thirty or so pieces, put the big sheet in front of her and let her lay the garden out before any glue comes near it.
Glue from the bottom up: stems first, then leaves, then flower heads on top so they overlap.
Write what she calls each plant along the bottom edge in marker and read the row back to her.
main.tip: Her cuts will be an inch long and jagged for months yet. Give her paper thin enough to cut and plenty to waste, and the wrist sorts itself out.

outside.title: Looking for the First Green
paras: Late February is where green comes back, so go and find it. Bulb shoots in the flower beds, moss in the cracks of a wall, an evergreen shrub, crocus tips where the sun reaches a south-facing wall. Give her a job: pick one real leaf to bring home and glue into the yard.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months. Give him a whole sheet of paper, too big to get into his mouth, and let him crush it. The noise arrives at the same instant his hand closes, the connection he is chasing this month. Soggy paper comes off him before he swallows any.

second.title: The Color Mailbox
second.intro: Every scrap she cut this morning is still on the floor. A shoebox with three slots in the lid turns the clearing up into the afternoon.
materials: 1 shoebox with a lid
1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
The paper offcuts from this morning
3 scraps of colored paper to label the slots
Masking tape
1 permanent marker
1 larger box with one wide slot, for Kreston
steps: Cut three slots in the lid, each a finger wide and about as long as your hand. Run masking tape along the cut edges so nobody gets a paper cut.
Tape a red, a yellow and a blue scrap beside the three slots.
Sweep the morning's offcuts into a bowl and put the bowl in her lap.
She posts. Red through red, yellow through yellow. The awkward ones (a photo of a dog, a black-and-white page) go wherever she argues for, and let the argument run.
Lift the lid, tip the lot out and do it again, four or five times.
On the last round, count them in out loud as she posts. Ten reds, six yellows, however many blues.
Sweep the small scraps up and lift Azlyn's bowl onto the table, then set Kreston's own box down where he can reach it, one wide slot and pieces too big to swallow.
second.tip: Let the wrong ones stay wrong. A page she calls red because the dog on it wears a red collar is a decision made from evidence, and she sharpens the rule herself over the next two weeks.

alternatives: Post plastic lids from the recycling into a coffee can with a slot cut in the lid.
Sort the crayon box by color into an ice cube tray.
Cut one page of the garden and stop there.
Feed scraps into a paper bag and shake it like a rattle.
outAgain: The pet store and the garden center, for the fish tank and the warm greenhouse
The park, if the wind has dropped
A thrift store for a bag of colored paper and a look at the toy shelf
A drive with the good radio station on
The corner store, and she carries one thing home
days.krestonPM: He comes to the garden center in the carrier facing out. Fish tanks hold an 8-month-old longer than anything else in the building, so park in front of one and let him watch. Back home he gets the big box and the fat offcuts.

insight.headline: Posting things through slots is a real developmental stage.
paras: Azlyn spent most of last year pushing objects into gaps, and Kreston is starting on it now. Psychologists call the pattern a schema, an action a child repeats to test one idea, and posting is among the most reliable. She is working out that her hand can aim at a target, that a shape either fits or it does not, and that a thing she cannot see is still somewhere, which she settled as a baby and is now checking against harder cases. Three-year-olds come back to the game when the sorting gets harder, which is why three colored slots hold her today far longer than a plain box would have last winter.

days.safety: Scissors, and small paper scraps on the floor with a crawling baby. The adult scissors and the craft knife go back up on a shelf between cuts, not onto the arm of the sofa. Sweep the floor before Kreston is put down. Check the shoebox for staples and tape every cut edge.

days.title: Everybody's Face
days.prepTonight: Check you have 2 cups of flour and 1 cup of salt in for this afternoon, and stand a chair where the morning light comes in with the hand mirror on it.

opening.title: Counting What's on a Face
steps: Hand her the mirror and give her a minute with it before you ask for anything.
Count a face out loud together: two eyes, one nose, one mouth, two ears, and however many teeth she claims to have.
Let her count yours, then Kreston's, then the cat's or the teddy's. Leave the mirror on the table. She needs it again at 9:15.

main.title: Sitting for a Portrait
materials: Thick card or paper, one sheet per person
Crayons and markers
1 hand mirror
1 permanent marker for names
Masking tape
A chair set where the light is good
steps: Tape a sheet of card to the table so it cannot slide while she works.
You sit first. Two minutes on the clock, chin up, and let her stare as long as she wants. Keep your eyes off her paper.
She says when it is finished. Write your name on it in marker while she watches.
Swap over and let her sit for you. Hand yours across whatever it looks like, and let her have opinions.
Kreston next. Two minutes of a baby holding still does not exist, so let her draw him mid-wriggle and put his name on it anyway.
Last one is herself, mirror propped against the fruit bowl. Three or four portraits by 10:15.
main.tip: A three-year-old draws a head with legs coming out of the chin. It has a name (the tadpole figure), and the body turns up around four.

outside.title: Finding Faces in Things
paras: Faces are hiding all over the street once she is looking. Two upstairs windows and a front door make a face on a house, and a car has eyes and a mouth from the front. Knots in a fence panel, a drain cover, the two bolts and a slot on a mailbox. Photograph the good ones and look back through them in the bath tonight.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months, and faces are most of what he studies. Prop the hand mirror in front of him and let him pat the glass and lean into it. He knows your face and Azlyn's cold, and he is busy sorting everyone else into safe or not. Let Azlyn hold her portrait of him up close and watch him reach for it.

second.title: The Dough Faces
second.intro: Salt dough holds a thumbprint, and a face made of lentils and buttons can be changed thirty times.
materials: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 cup salt, 1 cup water, 1 tablespoon oil
1 mixing bowl and a wooden spoon
Dried pasta, lentils and dried beans
Buttons if you have a jar of them
Yarn or string cut into short lengths for hair
1 dinner plate each as a work surface
1 table knife
Washable paint and a wide brush
1 sheet of thick card for the February handprint
1 wet washcloth
1 permanent marker
1 pencil, if you are marking the door frame this month
steps: Card and paint first, while her hands are clean. Paint her palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat, count to three, lift straight up. Write February and 3 beside it. Second of twelve.

Do Kreston's on the same sheet while he is calm, washcloth already in your hand, and 8 months beside his. If February is a month you want on the door frame, take both marks in pencil now while they are standing still, with the name and the date beside each.
Wash her hands, then flour and salt in the bowl, oil in, water in stages while she stirs. She decides when it stops sticking. Knead it on the table for five minutes between you, claggy to smooth.
Split it into balls, one for each person in the house. She flattens each into a round the size of her palm on its own plate.
Put the pasta, lentils, beans, buttons and yarn out in separate piles where she can see them all at once.
One plate at a time, and ask who it is before she starts. A named face gets eyebrows and hair. An unnamed one gets a handful of lentils.
Photograph the finished set, let her squash one flat and rebuild it as somebody else, then bag the leftover dough. The faces dry hard on a windowsill in two or three days.
second.tip: Give her the yarn last. Hair is the part she will spend twenty minutes on, and it goes on better once the eyes and mouth have settled.

alternatives: Draw faces on hard-boiled eggs and stand them in the egg cups.
Play dough faces from the tub you already own.
Build a face out of what is on the lunch plate before she eats it.
outAgain: Feeding the ducks, with yesterday's crusts and a look at how many are paired up now
A long loop with the stroller and no destination
The playground, for twenty minutes of climbing
The riverside path, to see how high the water is after the wet week
A drive to somewhere with a view and stay in the warm car
days.krestonPM: At 8 months he gets a fistful of dough shut in a small rigid pot with the lid taped on hard, to shove around the tray of his chair. Salt dough is dangerous eaten and a food bag is a suffocation risk at his age, so it is the pot, and the pot comes back when you stop watching. At the pond, keep him on you rather than at duck height. Ducks come at a sitting baby fast.

insight.headline: Love is a word she's still working out the size of.
paras: Azlyn will tell you she loves you, and then that she loves the yellow crayon, in the same voice. She is working with the word she has. A three-year-old sorts feeling into a few big bins before she gets the small ones, so love stretches across everything from you to a cookie, and the finer words (like, miss, prefer, want) arrive across the next two years. Drawing everyone in the house and naming each face is her drawing the circle. Keep handing her sharper words inside your own sentences, as in you missed Daddy today, and she picks them up when she needs them.

days.safety: Lentils, dried beans, buttons and pasta are choking hazards and every one of them ends up on the floor within reach of a baby who crawls. Sweep before Kreston goes down. Salt dough is dangerous eaten, so keep his hands out of the bowl and give him his own pot with the lid taped on.

days.title: The Cave Wall
days.prepTonight: Flatten two big boxes or dig out the brown kraft paper, stand it by the dining table with the masking tape, and check the flashlight batteries.

opening.title: Papering the Cave
opening.need: brown kraft paper or flattened boxes · masking tape · 1 flashlight.
steps: Clear everything out from under the dining table and get down there with her.
Tape paper to the underside of the table top and down the inside of the legs. You do the high bits, she does the low ones, and the wonky ones stay wonky.
Turn the big light off and hand her the flashlight. Let her look at the blank walls for a minute.

main.title: Painting on the Cave Wall
materials: Brown kraft paper or flattened cardboard boxes
Masking tape
1 flashlight with fresh batteries
Cocoa powder, 3 tablespoons
Paprika or turmeric, 2 tablespoons (substitute: mud from the yard, or black paint on its own)
Black washable poster paint
2 small bowls and 1 old toothbrush
1 kitchen sponge cut in half
Newspaper, a stack
An old T-shirt she can ruin
steps: Old T-shirt on, then mix the paints on the table out of her reach: cocoa and water in one bowl, paprika or turmeric and water in the other, black poster paint straight from the pot. Everything from here happens lying down or sitting on the floor.
Sponge first. Half a sponge loaded with cocoa and pressed flat gives a big soft brown mark.
Now the hand. Press her palm flat on the paper, hold it there, and dab paint around the edge. Lift straight up and the shape of her hand stays behind.
Newspaper down. Load the old toothbrush with spice paint and show her how to drag a thumb back across the bristles, spattering dots up the wall.
Do one handprint of yours beside hers, and Kreston's on a loose sheet if he will hold still.
Lights off, flashlight on, and look at the whole wall by flashlight. Ask her what happened in this cave and listen without adding to it.
main.tip: The toothbrush throws spice paint further than you think. Lay the newspaper wider than seems necessary.

outside.title: Digging for Color
paras: Take a trowel and a bag and go looking for ground that makes a mark. February ground is wet all the way through, so it gives under the blade. Look for red-brown clay a shovel down, pale chalky stone and charcoal from a cold fire site. Rub each find on a paving stone, and whatever leaves a color comes home in the bag.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and he will crawl straight under the table after her. Give him the flashlight beam to chase across the paper while the bowls stay up above. A moving light outranks everything else for his attention this month.

second.title: Paint Made of Mud
second.intro: The bag from this morning holds mud, stone and burnt wood, none of it paint yet.
materials: The mud, chalky stone and charcoal she collected
2–3 old plastic tubs
1 smooth stone or the back of a metal spoon for grinding
1 sieve or a tea strainer
Water in a pitcher
2 tablespoons all-purpose flour as a binder
Sticks and 1 old brush
Big paper or another flattened box
Old clothes and a towel by the sink
steps: Work at the sink or out on the step, because the next ninety minutes are dirty.
One tub per material. She breaks each lump down with the back of the spoon, and it takes real effort.
Sieve the powder into a clean tub. The fine dust is paint, and the grit left in the sieve goes in the trash.
Add water a spoonful at a time until it pours like cream, then a spoonful of flour so it grips the paper.
Test each tub with a stick on the box. Some give a strong color, some a smear of wet dirt, and she sorts them into two piles.
Line the good ones up and let her paint the big sheet with sticks and the old brush.
Wash in order: hands, then arms, then tubs. Tip the muddy water outside rather than down the sink.
second.tip: Mud from the top few inches is full of leaf and root and makes a weak smear. A trowel's depth down gives you clay.

alternatives: Cocoa and water on paper, nothing else added.
Draw with a stick of cold charcoal on the back of a cereal box.
Handprints in mud along the paving stones, hosed off after.
outAgain: The hill walk, for the view and the wind, hats on
The woods loop, to see what color the ground is up there
The riverside path, and check the water level again
Straight home to a warm bath, some Mondays
days.krestonPM: He comes on the hill walk in the carrier with a hat, facing in if the wind is up. At 8 months he sleeps most of the way back. At the sink he stays out of arm's reach of the tubs.

insight.headline: "A long time ago" is as much history as she can hold.
paras: Do not reach for forty thousand years today. Azlyn has no timeline yet, so last night, last summer and the Ice Age all sit together in one bin marked before. Children pick up past-tense language long before they can order events or judge how long anything lasted, and dates land on a three-year-old as noise. A long time ago, people lived in caves and painted on the walls with mud is the whole lesson and it is enough. Her hand pressed flat on the paper does the rest. Same hand, same wall, same idea, and she needs no number to feel it.

days.safety: Turmeric and paprika stain skin, grout and clothes, so keep them to paper and the old T-shirt. Kreston will crawl under the table and put a handful of spice paint or mud in his mouth, so the bowls live up on the table between uses. Wash every hand before food. Charcoal from a fire site only if it is cold all the way through.

days.title: Over, Under, Over
days.prepTonight: Dye the pasta tonight: a squirt of food coloring and a tablespoon of vinegar in a freezer bag per color, a handful of penne in, shake, then tip onto a tray lined with paper towels to dry overnight.

opening.title: Stringing the Loom
opening.need: 1 stiff cardboard rectangle · adult scissors (adult only) · yarn · masking tape.
steps: Cut notches along the top and bottom edges of the card, a finger's width apart and about half an inch deep. You cut, she counts them out loud.
Hook the yarn into the first notch, run it down to the notch opposite, round the back and up again. She holds the card steady while you wind.
Tape the loose end down at the back. It looks like a small harp now, and she can pluck it until 9:15.

main.title: Over and Under
materials: 1 stiff cardboard rectangle, roughly the size of a cereal box front
1 pair of adult scissors (adult only) for the notches
1 ball of yarn or string
Strips cut from magazines, grocery bags and an old T-shirt
Masking tape, to wrap the end of the yarn into a stiff tip instead of a needle
2 clothespins to hold the ends
steps: Cut the strips before she sits down: magazine, grocery bag and old T-shirt, each a finger wide and longer than the loom is across.
Wrap one end of each strip in masking tape to make a stiff point, a needle's job at a size her hand can hold.
Say the words while she does the first row. Over, under, over, under. Three rows of that, then go quiet.
Row two has to start under wherever row one started over. She will get this wrong, and a wrong row still looks good.
Push each finished row up tight against the one above. The gaps close and the card disappears.
Clip the loose ends at the sides so nothing slides back out.
main.tip: The rhythm carries her further than the instruction does. Chant over-under while she works and her hand picks the pattern up before she can explain it.

outside.title: The Fence Weave
paras: Take a bag of long strips and go and weave the street. A chain-link fence, a gate, a railing, a bare hedge. Feed the strips, yarn and dead grass in and out of the gaps until a patch of color lands on a gray street. Leave it for whoever walks past next, and come back Thursday to see whether the wind took it.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months. Stuff a burp cloth into an empty wipes box and let him haul it out, then stuff it back in for him and watch him do it again. Pulling comes before pushing at this age.

second.title: One Necklace Each
second.intro: The pasta came out of the freezer bags last night in colors nothing in this kitchen has any right to be.
materials: Dried penne or rigatoni, dyed overnight
Food coloring and 1 tablespoon vinegar, 1 freezer bag per color
1 tray lined with paper towels
String or yarn, ends wrapped in tape
2 drinking straws cut into short segments
1 bowl per color
1 pair of child-safe scissors, for the straws
1 pair of adult scissors (adult only), for the string
steps: Tip each color into its own bowl and let her look at the whole set before she threads anything.
Cut each string a hand's length longer than it takes to go over a head, tape one end into a point, and tie a piece of pasta at the far end so nothing slides off.
Let her cut the straws into short segments with her own scissors. She will do forty given the chance.
Thread. Pasta, straw, pasta, straw if she wants a pattern, any order at all if she does not.
One necklace per person, and ask who each one is for before she starts. The colors are her decision.
Knot every finished one loose enough to pull straight off, tested on your own head first.

Hand them out before dinner and put each one on the person she made it for. Kreston's hangs on a hook above adult head height where he can see it from the floor, never on a door handle, a crib rail or a chair back.
second.tip: Thread the first three yourself while she watches your hands. Stiff string aimed into a small hole, seen once at half speed, beats telling her to aim.

alternatives: Thread cereal hoops instead and eat the failures.
Weave paper strips through a sheet of paper with slits cut in it.
Thread buttons onto a shoelace.
outAgain: Swimming
The indoor play center if the pool session is canceled
The library, a day early
A warm café and a window, when nobody has it in them
days.krestonPM: At 8 months he sits supported in the water and slaps at the surface, and he will track Azlyn across the pool. Twenty minutes and out before he cools. The changing room is loud and full of strangers, so keep him against you while you wait in line.

insight.headline: Threading is fine motor work that pays off at six.
paras: Look at what her hands are doing this afternoon. One hand holds the string still while the other aims the pasta, thumb and forefinger pinched, both arms crossing the middle of her body to meet in front of her. Occupational therapists reach for threading because that combination is what a pencil grip is made of, and it takes years to build. None of it looks like schoolwork, which is why she comes back to it three times across an afternoon when a worksheet would have lasted two minutes. Years of this is what a hand needs before anybody asks it to write a page at six.

days.safety: Dry pasta and cut straw segments are the right size to choke an 8-month-old, and the floor is where they land. Sweep before Kreston goes down and keep his bowl separate. No cord or beaded necklace goes on a baby, awake or asleep. Knot Azlyn's loose enough to pull over her head, take them off before swimming and before bed, and keep the yarn and loose string up out of Kreston's reach all day. At the pool stay within arm's reach of both of them, close enough to take hold without a step, and hold Kreston or keep him in the stroller on the tiles.

days.title: A Picture for Somebody
days.prepTonight: Tip the crayon box out on the table with the coins, keys and a comb, and find four envelopes and two stamps for tomorrow afternoon's deliveries.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Quiet Corner and a Blanket

opening.title: Peeling the Crayons
opening.need: crayons nobody minds losing · 1 bowl · thin paper.
steps: Sit with her and peel the paper off. Fingernails only. She will keep at it long after you have had enough.
Snap the long ones in half and drop them in the bowl. A short crayon lies flat on its side.
Rub one flat across a scrap of paper laid over the edge of the table. Something comes up out of the page. Say nothing about how, and leave the bowl there until 9:15.

main.title: What's Under the Paper
materials: Crayons, wrappers peeled off and snapped in half
Printer paper or any thin paper, 15 sheets
Coins, keys, a fork, a comb
Leaves and a bit of bark
A sheet of sandpaper
The doormat, the radiator grille and a brick wall
Masking tape to hold the paper still
steps: Start with a coin, because a coin never fails. Tape a sheet of paper flat over it on all four edges.
Crayon held flat on its side, whole hand on top, rub back and forth. The coin comes up through the paper and she will stop dead.
Hand the choosing over. Fork, comb, keys, a leaf with the veins facing up, a piece of bark.
Take the paper to the thing when the thing will not come to you: the doormat, the radiator grille, the brick wall by the front door.
Sandpaper under the paper gives her a whole sheet of texture with no object in it, and she will want ten more.
Spread them on the floor and let her match each rubbing back to the thing that made it. You need four at 1:00, so keep the strong ones aside.
main.tip: Tape all four edges, every time. Most failed rubbings are the paper sliding, and she cannot hold it still and rub hard at once yet.

outside.title: The Sidewalk Rubbings
paras: Take paper, tape and half a dozen crayon stubs out with you. Drain covers, a water meter lid, a house number plate, the grain of a wooden bench, a memorial plaque, tree bark. February bark is soaked and will tear the paper, so pick a trunk on the dry side or go for metal. Carry them home flat in a bag rather than rolled.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and works everything out through his palms. Tape a square of sandpaper, a square of foil and a square of fleece onto a sheet of card and let him drag his hands across the three. Loose crayon stubs stay off the floor while he is down there.

second.title: Four Doors, Four Pictures
second.intro: Four of the rubbings go to four people this afternoon. She picks the pictures and the people.
materials: Four of her rubbings
4 envelopes, or folded paper and tape
Stamps for the ones going by post
1 pen, for the words she dictates
A shopping bag to carry them flat
The stroller
steps: Spread the morning's rubbings out and let her choose four. Take her choices even when she picks the four you would have thrown out.
Ask who each one is for. Say the four names back to her: a neighbor, a grandparent, somebody at playgroup, the friend two streets over.
Ask what she wants to say about each one. Write her words on the back as they come out, then read them back to her.
Fold each one into an envelope. She licks the flap and presses it shut, then draws on the front.
Write the names on the front in big letters and let her point to the first letter of each.
Coats on, stroller out. Deliver the ones you can walk to and let her push each envelope through the mail slot or into a hand.
The rest go to the mailbox with stamps on. She mails them, and you tell her how many sleeps until they land.
second.tip: Do the hand-delivered ones before the mailbox. Letters that vanish into a blue collection box make more sense once she has watched one arrive at a real door.

alternatives: Rubbings only. Deliver them tomorrow.
Draw a picture each for four people instead.
Photograph a rubbing and send it to somebody who will reply.
One huge rubbing on butcher paper, given to the house.
outAgain: The indoor play center, the quiet session, and go in the first ten minutes
The library, if this is a library week
The park for a run, if the rain holds off
A café with a window seat and something to watch
The bakery, and she chooses what everyone eats at four
days.krestonPM: He rides the delivery round in the stroller with the rain cover ready. At 8 months the quiet play-center session suits him, and he will crawl the length of a padded mat if you set him down at one end. Neighbors lean into a stroller at the door, so turn him to face you when they do.

insight.headline: Children need to see the effect of their kindness.
paras: Azlyn hands a neighbor a picture and watches a face open up. That reaction teaches her far more than being told afterwards that she was kind. Under-fours build a sense of themselves as someone who gives out of the response arriving while the giving is still happening, which is why the hand-delivered picture does more work than the posted one. The posted ones matter too, and they teach a slower lesson about a thing that travels out of sight and lands somewhere else. Give her both this afternoon, and make sure she is standing there when at least one door opens.

days.safety: Crayon stubs, coins and keys are all choking size, so they come off the floor and the room gets swept before Kreston is put down. Check the radiator is cold or turned off before she rubs it. Tape every foil edge flat on the texture board, and stay with him while he has it.

days.title: The Gallery Opens
days.prepTonight: Gather the whole week into one pile: the mixed-color paintings, the wet-paper ones, the cut-out garden, the portraits, the cave sheets, the woven card and the rubbings. Check you have masking tape.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Ones That Go on the Wall

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Looking at It from the Street

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Laying the Table for a Guest

opening.title: The Ones That Go on the Wall
opening.need: the week's work in one pile · a clear stretch of floor.
steps: Lay the whole week out on the floor in one long line. Six days of it.
Ask her to pick the ones that go on the wall. Take every choice, and take the rejections without arguing.
Count the chosen ones and put them in the order she wants them hung. That order is fixed from now until 10:15.

main.title: Hanging the Exhibition
materials: The week's paintings, cut-outs, rubbings, portraits and the woven card
Masking tape
String and 8 clothespins (hung above adult head height)
Card offcuts cut into label-sized rectangles
1 permanent marker
A chair for you, for the high ones
steps: Pick the wall. Somewhere Joseph walks past on his way in, and somewhere the light reaches.
Start at her eye level and build upward, taping the low ones and clipping the high row to the string. The bottom row is hers to hang and reach, the top row is yours off the chair.
Straighten every piece as it goes up. A straight row turns a wall of paper into an exhibition.
Cut the card into labels. Ask her what each piece is and write her answer down, then her name and the day she made it.
Tape each label under its picture. Walk the wall from end to end and read the whole thing back to her.
Stand at the far side of the room together and look at the week.
main.tip: Write her titles as she says them, the nonsense ones included. Green one that went wrong under a painting is worth more in ten years than Painting, February.

outside.title: Looking at It from the Street
paras: Go out the front and look back at your own window from the sidewalk, then walk the block and see what other people put in theirs. Cards on a sill, a child's drawing taped up, a plant, a cat asleep on a radiator. Count the windows with something in them. Wave at your own house on the way back in.

days.infant: Kreston is 8 months and hangs on to whatever he can reach. Tape one of Azlyn's paintings low on a wall or a cupboard door at his level, well away from the string, and let him crawl over and pat it. Azlyn chooses which one is his.

second.title: What Joseph Will Say
second.intro: One person in this house has not seen a single thing she made this week. The afternoon aims at the moment he walks through the door.
materials: Card for tickets and a door sign
1 permanent marker and masking tape
1 sheet of paper, folded, for her prediction
Cookies on a plate, a pitcher of water and plastic cups
A chair placed as the gallery seat
The hung exhibition
steps: Make the door sign together. She dictates the words, you write them, and she signs underneath with whatever she thinks her name looks like.
Cut tickets from the card, one for every person coming, and let her decide who is allowed in. Kreston gets one too.
Set the room up: the chair facing the wall, cookies on a plate, the pitcher and the cups on the table.
Walk the room the way a visitor would. In through the door, and ask what he sees first. Move things until she is happy with the order.
Ask her which picture Joseph will like best. Take the first answer and do not steer it.
Write her guess on the paper, fold it twice in front of her, and slide it under the cookie plate. It stays there until he is in the room.
Say nothing as he comes in and let her run the tour herself. Open the paper at the end and find out together.
second.tip: Tell Joseph nothing beyond what time he needs to be home. She wants a reaction nobody rehearsed, and he will give her a better one walking in cold.

alternatives: Tickets and cookies, no wall. Tour the pile on the table.
Phone a grandparent and carry the camera along the wall.
Draw the gallery from the doorway, wall and all.
Put one piece in a real frame and hang it in the hall for good.
outAgain: The pharmacy and a park bench, with the prescription and a bag of chips
The corner store for the cookies, and she picks them
The park, for a run before the gallery opens
Past Tuesday's fence weave, to see whether it survived
A short loop with the stroller if the rain has set in
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pharmacy in the carrier. At 8 months a line full of strangers leaning in is hard work, so face him inward and let him hide in your shoulder. He gets his ticket in your lap and he will try to eat it. Sit him where he can watch the tour go past.

insight.headline: Anticipating someone else's future feeling is a big cognitive leap.
paras: Guessing which picture Joseph will like asks a great deal of a three-year-old. She has to hold a mind that is not hers, load it with preferences that differ from her own, and run it forward into an evening that has not happened yet. Most children get good at that around four, so today she will pick her own favorite and be taken aback when he chooses another. The guess is worth making whether or not it lands. Sealing it under the cookie plate gives her a before and an after to compare, and comparing those two is where the skill grows.

days.safety: The clipped string comes down the moment the tour is over, and it never hangs anywhere either child can reach. Use plastic cups rather than glasses with Kreston loose on the floor. His ticket stays in your lap, and it comes back before it is chewed small enough to swallow.
